title: Statistics: are Stehle's DIAWINFBN run and the mod-7 doublets real?
why: Two famous K4 oddities nobody has put a corrected p-value on. Cheap; tells us whether to chase 4- or 7-spaced structure.

title: Sanborn's 2025 hints as keywords everywhere (Quagmire I-IV + theme-keyword columnar x all key models)
why: Newest clues (Egypt 1986, Berlin Wall, delivering a message, World Clock) are barely mined.

title: Decimation (97 is prime), grid routes, K3 rotations x every key model
why: Others tried these scrambles with repeating keys only; progressive, autokey and digit keys behind them are untested.

title: Myszkowski from ~190k dictionary words x every key model
why: Myszkowski was only covered at widths 3-9 with a periodic key.

title: Columnar (every order, widths 2-11) + digit / small-shift key
why: Digit keys are dead alone but untested behind a transposition; fits Bean's 'letters sit close' finding.

title: Double columnar (widths 2-6 x 2-6) x progressive / autokey / digit keys
why: Attack 07 did double columnar with periodic keys only.

title: Columnar (every order, widths 2-10) + autokey (ciphertext or plaintext feeds the key)
why: Autokey alone is dead; stacked behind a transposition it is untested.

title: Columnar (every order, widths 2-10) + progressive key
why: Progressive alone is dead; stacked it is untested.

title: Keyword alphabets at key lengths 14-26, forced plaintext scored for English
why: Clue letters can't decide these lengths (open gap); English scoring against shuffled K4 can.

title: Double columnar width 8 x widths 2-6 + periodic key
why: Pushes attack 07 one width further.

title: Fingerprint ranking: which cipher families produce K4-like statistics?
why: No key search. Ranks ~30 families by how often their output shows K4's oddities (flat IoC, lag-4 run, mod-7 doublets, width-21 repeats, close letters), as a soft prior for where to search next.

title: Practice puzzles: decrypt PK1-PK9 from the public keys, test our blind solvers
why: Ground truth for calibration: shows how far our toolkit reaches on Paradigm's idea of 'Kryptos-like' ciphers.

title: Quagmire I/II (one hidden alphabet) at every key length; undecidable lengths completed by annealing
why: Lengths 13, 16, 19, 20, 23, 24, 26 can't be decided by the clues (open gap); English completion vs planted and shuffled controls can.

title: Gromark / chain-addition keys with both alphabets hidden; survivors completed by annealing
why: A top fingerprint family. Bean's 39 survivors 'can be completed several ways' - this does the completion and compares with controls.

title: Fingerprint ranking again, with the new hidden-alphabet families
why: Do Gromark-with-hidden-alphabets and Quagmire I/II/IV look K4-like?

title: LAYER TWO: two stacked repeating keys, every length pair <=26, completed by annealing
why: Stacked keys (PK3/PK8 style, K2's 'LAYER TWO') give a key that never repeats inside 97 letters on a plain alphabet. The undecidable pairs were never completed.

title: Three layers: a theme word plus two unknown keys (fully clue-determined configs)
why: PK8 stacked four keys; with one layer a known theme word the rest is exactly solvable.

title: K1-K3 misspellings (L/Q, O/U, E/A, S/C) as alphabet swaps x key models and two stacked keys
why: Sanborn: K1-K3 answers hold clues and the misspellings are deliberate; as alphabet swaps they give the near-plain alphabets our fingerprint favours. Untested in this form.

title: World Clock (Weltzeituhr) as of 1989: city names, initials and UTC offsets as keys
why: Sanborn (2025): BERLINCLOCK = the World Clock at Alexanderplatz and the 1989 Wall fall matters. Everyone used the post-1997 plates; we reconstructed the 1989 ones from dated photos.

title: Visual letter transforms: semaphore rotations/mirrors and Morse reverse/invert, alone or stacked with key layers
why: Sanborn's 'visual systems'; semaphore is two hands on a dial (Berlin Clock-shaped). Never tested.

title: Compass-bearing keys read across the exact carved layout (cipher panel, tableau, mirrored tableau)
why: EAST NORTHEAST is in the clue; physical/visual steps; uses the verified carved line layout.

title: SLM cipher detective: small neural net trained on ~100k synthetic K4-like ciphertexts names K4's family
why: A learned, richer version of the fingerprint ranking; training on K4 itself can't work (97 letters).

title: Local LLM (Qwen2.5-7B) as English judge for the blind stacked-key region, plus what it generates as K4
why: Quadgrams can't tell real from fake English where ~20 key letters are free; an LLM judge might, calibrated on planted vs shuffled.

title: Key-shape forensics: period signatures in letter differences; could the key be a slowly turning dial?
why: NSA's 'pattern every 7', the mod-7 doublets, Bean's width 21 and the neural detective's 'progressive' all hint at key shape.

title: Self-masking: K4 keyed by its own plaintext or ciphertext read in a scrambled order
why: Scheidt's 'masking' on a plain alphabet; natural-order self-keying (autokey) is dead, scrambled never tried.

title: Baudot/Vernam teleprinter cipher (ITA2 XOR): periodic, stacked, autokey, word and text keys
why: K2's 'transmitted underground' = the CIA Berlin Tunnel tapping teleprinter lines; never tested on K4.

title: Lorenz-style teleprinter wheels: each of the 5 bits with its own short repeating wheel
why: The Cold War teleprinter machine family; each bit plane is exactly testable on its own.

title: Paper strips: K4's carved rows or equal-width strips, reordered and flipped, x every key model
why: Kobek found the plaintext as strips taped out of order; the verified carved layout gives the strips.

title: Egypt-era alphabets (hieroglyph, Coptic, Greek, Phoenician, Arabic orders) x key models, Quagmire, stacked keys
why: Sanborn: the 1986 Egypt trip figures in the solution; near-plain alphabets are what the fingerprint favours.

title: Shifting matrices / number-base change: grid coordinates each shifted by its own wheel
why: Sanborn: 'matrix codes Ed gave me'; Scheidt: 'a different math base', 'shifting matrices'. Only the base-3 cube with simple keys was tried.

title: Gromark in other number bases (3-16), both alphabets hidden, completed
why: Scheidt's 'different math base'; Bean/Barney list survivors in base 8 etc.; completions never done.

title: Long stacked keys revisited: heat-bath solver + English-key prior
why: Diagnosis showed the open region is search-limited (true answers score higher than what was found), not information-limited.

title: Selective masking: KRYPTOS letters lightly shifted, the rest keyed
why: 9/10 KRYPTOS-letter clues shift <=2 (shuffled p~0.003); maybe the keyword decides which letters get the real key.

title: Key restarts at each sentence (+X separators), 18 alphabets
why: Plaintext = sentence strips; K1-K3 use X between sentences; Cyrillic Projector restarts its key per block.

title: A different simple system for each part (split 34-63)
why: 'Two separate systems' read literally: one for the EASTNORTHEAST part, another for the BERLINCLOCK part.

title: One deliberate mistake: drop-one-clue for periodic, two keys, hidden-alphabet Gromark
why: Sanborn's work is 'rife with mistakes on purpose'; one wrong clue letter makes exact tests reject the true method.

title: KRYPTOS-letter masking inside the clue sentences + restarting key (pre-filter hybrid)
why: Clue matrix: selective masking explains the KRYPTOS closeness but breaks flatness unless <=~20 letters are masked; top hybrid = masking x sentence restarts.

title: Two stacked keys that are both real words/phrases/dates (+ one-wrong-clue pass)
why: Round 6: long stacked keys are information-limited; hand keys are words (PALIMPSEST, ABSCISSA), which removes every free slot.

title: Three layers: theme word + two word keys
why: Same, with a theme word (Berlin/Egypt/clock/K1-K3) as a third layer; three-stage stacks are a listed community gap.

title: K1-K3 plaintexts as keys with hidden alphabets (4 models)
why: 'Answers to K1-K3 contain clues to K4'; text keys were only tried on A-Z/KRYPTOS alphabets.

title: Clock arithmetic keys (dials 12/24/60, two hands) + carved-row restarts
why: 'Delve into that particular clock': a clock is modular arithmetic; carved row 4 restarts inside BERLINCLOCK, which idea 43 couldn't test.

title: Letter class picks the table (KRYPTOS letters on the KRYPTOS tableau)
why: KRYPTOS-letter clues behave differently; two tables by letter class is a fully keyed version that can stay flat.

title: Second look at every saved candidate (big model, word coverage, LLM judge)
why: Every candidate was judged by one score at the time; re-judge all together, calibrated on real English with forced clues.

title: Formula mining: every 0-4 ingredient linear formula for the key
why: Earlier rounds tested named key rules one at a time; this tests every short combination of 186 ingredients at once.

title: Autokey / Condi / Ragbaby with a hidden alphabet (exact linear solve)
why: Autokey was only ruled out on known alphabets; the hidden alphabet drops out of a linear system mod 26.

title: Interrupted key: restart at a trigger letter or at each word
why: A classical hand cipher that hides the period; restarts were only tested at sentences and carved rows.

title: Sentence key (unknown English text) on keyword tableaux
why: K1/K2's own system with a different keyword and a whole-sentence key; the forced key letters must read as English.

title: The sculpture read other ways as the key (columns, diagonals, skips)
why: Sanborn's step is 'visual'; sculpture running keys were only read along the rows.

title: Autokey stacked with a repeating key word (two systems)
why: The two simplest in-place hand systems stacked directly; only tested behind transpositions before.

title: Two systems in turn: switching rows, interleaved streams, Slidefair pairs
why: Three literal readings of 'two separate systems' that round 7 did not cover.

title: Scrambled key: K3's transposition applied to the repeating key, text left in place
why: Uses both of the lower half's systems while keeping BERLINCLOCK in place, which text transpositions cannot.

title: Drifting key word (each key letter steps at its own rate) + the EAST/EAST near-repeat measured
why: EAST encrypts to FLRV and, 9 letters on, to GKSS: nearly the same. Tests the model that suggests.

title: Three remembered key words: Quagmire IV over all dictionary alphabet pairs (hash join)
why: Scheidt: simple, remembered, 'with the correct key word/s'. K1/K2's machine with three words instead of two.

title: The '?' counts: 98 = 7 x 14 cells (reruns of 54, 61, 62 with KRYPTOS_QMARK=1)
why: Scheidt: special characters must be accounted for. With the ? K4 is an exact grid; 97 alone is prime.

title: Chain-addition key in letters; row word + column word grids
why: Ways an agent stretches a remembered word into a long key; clue blocks start 42 apart = K3 worksheet width.

title: Every dictionary keyword tableau x battery of key rules (sliding, stacked, autokey...)
why: Round 9's key rules were only run on the A-Z and KRYPTOS tableaux; the tableau keyword may be another word.

title: Carter's reply as a guessed third clue; undecided models re-run
why: K3 ends with a question and K4 starts where the answer would; 18 more letters make undecidable models decidable.

title: Each clue alone, and both clues with the gap off by 1-3 letters
why: Sanborn dropped a letter carving K2; every joint test assumes the 42-letter gap between the clues is exact.

title: Rows of 21: column key shared by the two clue rows, row decides offset or tableau
why: Both clues start a row in a 21-wide grid (K3's worksheet was 42 wide); 'ID BY ROWS'.

title: Wrong modulus: key arithmetic on a wheel of 27-31 cells
why: Scheidt: special characters must be accounted for (27 symbols with '?'); the carved tableau rows are 30-31 wide.

title: Multiplier word + adder word (C = A*P + B, both repeating)
why: Decimated alphabets are as easy by hand as shifted ones; only one fixed multiplier had been allowed.

title: Paper rotor: hidden wiring between two alphabets, turned by a key word
why: Not linear in a hidden alphabet, so unseen by every earlier exact test; others tried only constant-speed rotors.

title: Evolving alphabet: the alphabet changes after every letter
why: A one-sentence hand rule with flat statistics and no period; decrypts from letter 0 with no unknown plaintext.

title: Autokey with a keyed distance (a pattern says how far back to look)
why: All earlier autokey tests used one fixed lag.

title: Wheatstone clock-face cipher with any rings (proof + dictionary cross-check)
why: BERLIN CLOCK, a 27th symbol; the repeated cipher letters S,S and R,R decide it for every ring.

title: Digital interpretation: letters as 5 bits (binary, Gray, Bacon), Morse as a switch
why: DIGETAL INTERPRETATU; only Baudot numbering had been tested.

title: Tableau seen through the pierced copper: mirrored, flipped, slanted overlays
why: SHADOW FORCES, 'it's visual'; round 9 read the panels as text but not as a mirrored overlay.

title: Round 11 battery (68 clue alone / gap slack, 70 mod 27-31, 71B fixed multipliers, 74 keyed-lag autokey) on 446,675 transposition-mixed keyword alphabets
why: Ideas 68, 70, 71 and 74 used the 220k plain keyword alphabets; round 10 showed the two transposition-mixed forms triple the alphabet set and are how a keyword alphabet is often built by hand.

title: German sentence keys on keyword tableaux: not run, the repository has no German language model
why: BERLIN CLOCK and the 1989 Berlin setting make German text a natural running key; attack 57 scored forced key fragments only against English.

title: Gap between the clues off by 1-3 letters: formula mining (54, sizes 0-3) and the three-keyword Quagmire IV hash join (63, key lengths 1-20)
why: Idea 68 showed nothing with the gap between the clues off by 1-3 letters, but only for the key-rule battery. Formula mining (54) and the Quagmire IV hash join (63) also tie the two clues together through absolute positions.

title: One wrong clue letter: key-rule battery, multiplier+adder words (71A) and word-turned rotor (72) on every 23 of the 24 clue letters
why: Sanborn's texts carry deliberate misspellings (IQLUSION, UNDERGRUUND, DESPARATLY). Round 7 tested one wrong clue letter only for periodic, two-key and Gromark models.

title: Two paper rotors in series: two different hidden wirings (form H, mostly cannot be judged) and one hidden strip used there and back (form B, dead)
why: Idea 72 closed one rotor with hidden wiring. Two rotors is the smallest machine that idea cannot see, and the wire-collision test extends to it when the slow rotor moves rarely.

title: Any state machine moved by a hidden table of the letter (cipher = F(state), state += g(letter) mod m, m = 2..60): the plain pair S,T is doubled once and not doubled once
why: The Wheatstone proof (idea 75) used only this: plain S then T gives cipher S,S at letters 32-33, and plain S ... T gives cipher R,R at letters 23 and 28. Any state machine must treat T after S,T,N,O,R as it treated S.

title: Two repeating-key layers on two different tableaux (A-Z, KRYPTOS, theme and dictionary keyword alphabets), exact test on the clue letters
why: K2 ends LAYER TWO and Scheidt calls K4 'more than one stage'. Every stacked-key test so far put both layers on the same tableau, where the two keys simply add. A KRYPTOS-tableau layer followed by an A-Z layer (or any two different keyword tableaux) is not a sum of keys on any single alphabet, so none of the earlier exact tests can see it.

title: K4 letters as skip counts through the sculpture's own text: moving window (rule A) and pointer walk (rule B) over 39 texts
why: Sanborn 2019: no particular book is needed, 'just to be able to read'; 2025: 'Who says it is even a math solution?'; 2005-2006: the earlier passages hold instructions and clues for the fourth. A reading method fits all three: each K4 letter says how far to count on (A=1..Z=26) through K1-K3 to reach the next plaintext letter. The encoder can choose among occurrences, which flattens the letter counts (masking) and lets S give S. Every earlier test treats the cipher letter as a letter added to a key, never as a distance.

title: Any keyword alphabet (keyword of 1-25 different letters, then A-Z), solved exactly from the clue equations with no dictionary: Quagmire III/I/II, repeating key 1-26 and sliding key period 1-26
why: Scheidt: K4 runs 'with the correct key word/s', and K1's own keyword was a misspelling (PALIMPCEST). Every keyword-tableau test used about 220k dictionary words, so a name, a German word, a misspelling or a short phrase as the alphabet keyword was never tested. A keyword alphabet is far from arbitrary: after the keyword's letters the rest run in A-Z order, and that gives enough extra equations to decide key lengths where the arbitrary-alphabet tests could not (13, 16, 18-20, 23, 24, 26).

title: Spaces use up key letters: key-rule battery with the key slipping one place per word break (3 x 2 clue parsings, extra offset 0-25)
why: Scheidt 2015: 'special characters don't work' and must be accounted for. If Sanborn enciphered from a sheet with word spaces and the key ran on over each space, the key position is the letter number plus the number of word breaks so far. Our tests restarted keys at words (idea 56) or moved the second clue by up to 3 places (idea 68), but never let the key slip one place per word inside the clues.

title: Autokey one worksheet row back: plain feed at lags 7, 8 and 34-48 (first clue keys the second, second clue moved -3..3), cipher feed at lags 1-66, with a constant or a repeating word of 2-4 on top, on 666,993 keyword tableaux
why: The K3 worksheet is 42 wide and the two clues start exactly 42 apart; with the '?' K4 is a 7 x 14 grid and five of the six doubled letters end a row of 7. If each row is keyed by the row above (the letter 7 or 42 places back, plaintext or ciphertext), the first clue is the key for the second. The battery tried lags 1-6 only on keyword tableaux, and lags 30-52 got only a quick look on A-Z/KRYPTOS (3 of 6).

title: 140,752 alphabets that are not keyword alphabets (first-appearance orders from the sculpture's texts, QWERTY, Morse and frequency orders): key-rule battery, sentence-key score, and two-alphabet join for key lengths 1-20
why: Every exact test since round 9 drew its alphabets from A-Z, KRYPTOS or dictionary keywords, and open_gaps lists non-keyword alphabets as still open. The hand-made alternatives are few and listable: a sentence's letters in order of first appearance (a keyphrase alphabet from K1-K3 or the Morse text; 'the answers to the first three passages contain clues to the fourth'), typewriter rows, Morse-code order (the entrance slabs), letter-frequency order.

title: Independent-encryptor audit: 678 K4-shaped messages from textbook encryptors (no shared code) fed to the test functions of attacks 63, 66, 71, 72, 74, 78
why: AGENTS.md: a search that cannot find a planted answer proves nothing. Every planted test so far was built with the attack's own helper code, so a shared mistake (clue positions off by one, an alphabet indexed the wrong way, a Beaufort sign) would pass its planted test and still miss the real K4. 343 negatives rest on those shared conventions.

title: Known word keys (264,828 words and K1-K3 phrases at every phase: repeating, sliding, progressive) and 45,104 sculpture readings as running keys, on one fully hidden alphabet: numeric key, true Quagmire III, true Quagmire II, hidden alphabet on one side
why: Scheidt: K4 runs 'with the correct key word/s'. open_gaps lists hidden-alphabet keys of 23+ letters as open, but only because the key letters were treated as unknowns. If the key is a dictionary word or a reading of the sculpture, the stream is known and one hidden alphabet is decidable at every key length. In true Quagmire III the key letter is found on the same hidden alphabet, so S->S (33) and K->K (74) force the key letters at those two places to be the same letter: a filter no earlier test used.

title: Key formulas of 0-3 ingredients (position, number sequences, grids of width 2-40, carved layout) with a hidden tableau alphabet: one hidden alphabet on both sides (Vigenere and Beaufort form) or on one side against A-Z / KRYPTOS
why: The fingerprint ranking names 'a structured key under an unknown mixed alphabet' as a top open target, and Sanborn's coding chart need not be a keyword alphabet. Idea 54 mined 9 million key formulas, but only on A-Z and KRYPTOS. A KNOWN key stream stays decidable when one hidden alphabet is used on both sides: the 24 clue letters tie 21 letters into one piece with 4 closed loops, and the 21 positions must all differ (chance about 1e-11 per stream, 4e-10 with a free constant).

title: Word autokey: each word is enciphered with the previous word (or the word two back) as key, plain or cipher letters, forwards or reversed, wrap or run-on, on 666,993 keyword tableaux, on any tableau, and on one hidden alphabet
why: Scheidt: 'simple, can be remembered'; he 'masked the English language'. A key that never repeats and needs no key text: after a primer word, each plaintext word is enciphered with the word before it. Inside the clues the previous word is known (EAST keys NORTH, NORTH keys EAST, BERLIN keys CLOCK), so there are up to 14 equations with no unknown key letter. The fixed-lag autokey tests (lags 1-6, and idea 74's repeating lag patterns) cannot see it because the lag changes with each word's length.

title: Message enciphered back to front: look-ahead autokey, plain feed d = 1-8 and 34-48 (second clue keys the first, moved -3..3), cipher feed d = 1-68, on 666,993 keyword tableaux; plus multiplier 1-25 with a word of 1-13 on A-Z/KRYPTOS, and one hidden alphabet at d = 1-8
why: Sanborn 2005: he left 'instructions in the earlier text that refer to later text'. If K4 was enciphered from its last letter backwards, an autokey takes its key from the letters that FOLLOW, and the second clue can be the key for the first (the blocks start 42 apart, the K3 worksheet width). Idea 54 covered neighbours 1-5 ahead on A-Z and KRYPTOS only; the keyword-tableau battery (66), the hidden-alphabet autokey (55), the stacked autokey (59) and idea 90 all look backwards.

title: Two rotors in series, one wired from a dictionary keyword strip and one hidden, in both orders
why: Idea 82 found that two hidden wirings (52 unknown contacts) cannot be judged from 24 letters, and its worker noted that with one wiring known the test turns into idea 72's wire test with about 8 forced coincidences. Scheidt's 'key word/s' fits a device with one remembered keyword strip and one chart Sanborn changed 'so that Scheidt could not decipher it'. Open after round 11: two rotors.

title: Key word on one tableau, steadily turning (shift s*i + t) second tableau, both orders, two different alphabets
why: K2 ends LAYER TWO; Scheidt taught 'shifting matrices' and calls K4 'more than one stage'. Idea 84 closed two repeating keys on two different tableaux and its worker noted the same test works when layer two is not periodic but known up to a few numbers. A steadily turning second tableau (shift s*i + t) is the simplest such layer, hides the period of the first, and was only ever tested with both layers on the same tableau, where it folds into one key.

title: A key written with few symbols (digits in any base, clock hours, Roman numerals): smallest window and number of distinct key values on 666,993 keyword tableaux, no rule for the key
why: Scheidt: 'I could have moved to a different math base' (2 to 16); Sanborn: 'delve into that particular clock' (clock faces carry numerals). A key that is a list of numbers, however irregular, uses few distinct values. The community showed no alphabet makes all 24 key values digits 0-9 or keeps them below 16, but only for a window starting at 0 and one way of naming the key letter. Any window of 12 or fewer values has a chance rate of 2e-7 per setting, so the question is decidable on every tableau with no rule for the key at all.

title: Plaintext autokey at a long lag, 9-33 letters back or ahead, decided by chains through the unknown letters, on 666,993 keyword tableaux
why: Bean measured 11 repeated vertical pairs at width 21, both clue blocks start a row of 21, and the K3 worksheet rows are 42 wide: a row keyed by the row above is plaintext autokey at a long lag. Idea 90 wrote that plain feed at lags 9-12 and 13-33 cannot be decided because few clue pairs sit exactly one lag apart. That misses chains: with a known tableau, a known letter and the cipher letter one lag on (or back) give the next plaintext letter, so each clue letter fixes its whole residue class and the classes of the two blocks meet. Counted: lag 9 has 15 checks, lag 13 has 11, lags 20 and 21 have 11, and lags 24-33 force 58-86 of the 97 letters.

title: Second pass of the key word differs: key read back and forth (and its sliding form), form alternating by pass, odd passes shifted by a constant, tableau alternating by pass, on 666,993 keyword tableaux
why: K1 key PALIMPSEST is a sheet written over a second time, K2 ends LAYER TWO, and Sanborn said the lower half uses two separate systems. A hand encoder who changes something each time the key word comes round (reads it backwards, switches from Vigenere to Beaufort, switches chart) gives a key of period 2L that no repeating-key test at length L sees, and for L = 14-24 the period is 28-48, outside every exact test so far. The mirror rule halves the unknowns: counted from the clue positions, a back-and-forth key has 7-11 checks at every period 28-46.

title: Half-hidden Quagmire IV: one dictionary keyword alphabet (666,993 incl. transposition-mixed), the other alphabet anything; repeating key of 1-12 unknown numbers or sliding key (running sum of an unknown word) of 1-9
why: Sanborn 2005: he modified the system 'so that Scheidt could not decipher it'; Scheidt: 'key word/s'. Idea 63 closed three dictionary words, idea 20 closed one hidden alphabet against A-Z or KRYPTOS, and idea 86 covers an unknown keyword alphabet. Nobody has tested a dictionary keyword alphabet on one side with a freely written alphabet on the other and a short repeating key. It is exact: with the plain side known the 14 cipher letters and L key letters leave 11 - L checks, plus the need for 14 different positions.

title: One place lost in the key inside a clue word: repeating and sliding keys with one key letter skipped or used twice inside EASTNORTHEAST or BERLINCLOCK
why: Sanborn dropped a letter carving K2, misspelled the K1 key on his own worksheet (PALIMPCEST) and calls his work rife with mistakes. In a hand Vigenere the commonest slip is losing the place in the key: one key letter skipped or repeated, after which every later letter is one place off. Idea 68 moved the whole second clue by 1-3 places, which covers slips BETWEEN the clues, and idea 81 dropped single clue letters, which covers one wrong letter; neither covers a slip that falls inside EASTNORTHEAST or BERLINCLOCK, where it breaks every periodic test.

title: Matrix codes on 26/27-cell rectangles (2x13, 13x2, 3x9, 9x3): any pair-for-pair substitution, two-square and four-square, pairing widths 1-48
why: Sanborn 2005: he used matrix codes Ed gave him. Scheidt 2015: special characters do not work and must be accounted for; with the carved ? K4 has 98 symbols = 49 pairs, and 26 letters + ? = 27 = 3 x 9. The negatives close Playfair, two-square and four-square only because a 5x5 square cannot output 26 letters, and Bean tested paired letters only at widths 7 and 21. Squares that are 2x13 or 3x9 rectangles keep all 26 letters, work on fixed pairs (so clue letters stay in place) and two-square can leave a letter unchanged (K to K).

title: Two stacked keys at every length pair the old pre-filter dropped (plain, gap slack, mod 27-31, fixed multipliers, one clue letter out, word breaks counted), and autokey / progressive key numbered on A-Z or KRYPTOS, on 666,993 keyword tableaux
why: Idea 91 fed 678 textbook-enciphered messages to the round 9-11 tests and attack 66 missed 115 that had enough checks. Two causes: (a) the stacked-key pre-filter adds two partial counts (c1 + c2 < 8) and wrongly drops 20 length pairs that the exact solve can judge; (b) autokey was tested only with the fed letter numbered on the tableau alphabet, not on A-Z, KRYPTOS or the other side (Quagmire I autokey as the ACA defines it, or rows picked by the A-Z labels as carved). Until these run, two stacked key words on a keyword tableau and plain autokey at lags 1-6 are not closed as the summaries say.

title: Independent-encryptor audit, part 2: 3,192 K4-shaped messages from textbook encryptors (no shared code) fed to the test functions of attacks 54, 56, 57, 59, 60, 61, 62, 65, 68, 69, 70, 73, 74, 78, 79, 81, 84, 86, 88, 89, 90, plus 918 messages mapping two stacked keys
why: Idea 91 was the only check so far that did not share code with the attacks, and it found two real scope holes in attack 66 that every planted test had passed. It reached six attacks. The other exact tests (rounds 9-10: 54-62, 65, 67; round 11: 69, 70, 73, 75-77; swarm: 79-90) still rest only on planted answers made by their own code, and every negative in the log that says autokey or stacked keys p < q <= 13 may repeat the same holes.

title: K4 letters as word counts through the K1-K3 plaintexts and the Morse text: walk (W), moving window (B) and letter pairs (C) over 56 word lists
why: Scheidt: K4 is like ciphers given to agents or pilots in case of capture, not mathematical, simple, can be remembered; the letter codes taught to air crews hid a message in an ordinary text and found it by counting words. Sanborn: the earlier text holds instructions for the later text, the first three answers contain clues to the fourth, and the solver needs just to be able to read. Idea 85 counted letters and showed a 26-letter window can hardly encode English; its worker noted that word counting can, because word starts are rich in the letters a message needs.

title: Strip moved by a text: first and second differences of the forced key (12+10 and 11+9 letters) against 198,934 sculpture readings and as unknown English, on 666,993 dictionary tableaux
why: Scheidt: simple, can be remembered, with the correct key word/s; Sanborn: just be able to read. Round 10 introduced the sliding key (each key letter says how far to MOVE the strip, so the key is the running sum of the word) but only for repeating words up to 17 letters. With a sentence or a sculpture reading as the moving text the key never repeats, the clues force 22 of its letters (the differences inside each block), and no earlier test looks at differences: attacks 57 and 58 compare the key letters themselves with text.

title: One word per worksheet line on 666,993 keyword tableaux: column key + a free letter per line, a speed per word, own speed and start per word, and a strip moved by the column key; 6 word-break parsings of the clues, column from word start or end, Vigenere / Beaufort / lines taking turns
why: The K4 plaintext survives as strips cut from a handwritten sheet, the K1 worksheet is written in short clusters, and the Cyrillic Projector restarts its key at each block. If the worksheet had one word per line, the key letter depends on the place inside the word, and each line may add its own letter (a row word down the side). Idea 66 tested a key that restarts at each word with nothing added and idea 65 tested row word + column word only on grids of fixed width; lines of ragged length were never tested. It is exact: for EAST / NORTH / EAST and BERLIN / CLOCK there are 10 unknown key letters against 24 clue letters, so 14 checks.

title: Each plain letter keeps its own counter into a key word (homophone cycling) on known keyword tableaux: dictionary words and K1-K3 phrases, any-letter keys to length 5, row restarts, 3-4 fixed alphabets in turn
why: Scheidt: I masked the English language, and the cipher is simple, remembered, run with the correct key word/s. The classic hand way to flatten letter counts while staying letter-for-letter is to give every plaintext letter its own counter: the first E takes key letter 1, the second E key letter 2, and so on. The key then depends on how often THAT letter has occurred, not on the position, which no earlier test models (idea 83 had one shared state, and its doubled-pair rule does not apply here).

title: Any linear key rule on a keyword tableau, with no rule named: order 5 with free coefficients (plus a drift term), text-fed rules with two key taps, and arbitrary tables of the key, plain or cipher letter 1-6 back
why: Scheidt: simple, can be remembered, run years later. Rounds 9-11 tested named key rules one by one (progressive, chain addition with two taps, formulas from a list). Every such rule, and any rule nobody listed, where each key letter is a fixed linear mix of the few key letters before it, obeys ONE linear recurrence, and that can be tested exactly without naming the rule. It also does not care where the clues sit, so it is immune to a wrong gap or a miscounted position.

title: Vowels and consonants keyed by two separate words (class by plain or cipher letter, Vigenere/Beaufort per class), and one key that holds or skips on a letter set, on 666,993 keyword tableaux
why: Sanborn 1990: two separate systems; Scheidt masked the English language and explains the problem as the E against the Z. A hand way to do both: two key words, one used up by the vowels and one by the consonants, each moving on only when it is used. The key place of a letter then depends on the text before it, so every position-based test of rounds 9-11 fails on such a message even with short words. Idea 60 split letters by position (odd and even), never by kind of letter; the community pause tests were on plain A-Z only.

title: Free choice per letter between Vigenere/Beaufort/variant (one tableau) or between two tableaux, with a repeating or sliding key, on 220,318 keyword alphabets
why: Scheidt 'masked the English language'; Sanborn 1990: 'two separate systems'; 2019: the solver needs 'just to be able to read'. If the encoder was free to use either of two systems for each letter, picking whichever flattens the counts, the reader tries both and keeps the one that reads. Idea 60 tested free switching between fixed rows and rule-based switching with keys, and the community tested a fixed form per key letter; a repeating key word with a free choice of form at every letter has not been tested.

title: Smallest window of the 24 clue key values that ANY hidden alphabet allows (exact), 7 layouts, all clues and each block alone
why: Bean: the clue plaintext and ciphertext letters sit unusually close in the alphabet (about 1 in 5,520), and the fingerprint ranking names small-shift keys under an unknown mixed alphabet as a top open target. Idea 97 measured the narrowest window of key values on 667k keyword tableaux (K4: 12, inside the controls) but only for listed alphabets. With the alphabet free it becomes a constraint problem that can be solved exactly.

title: Quagmire IV with both alphabets hidden, key of 8 (repeating, and sliding with word sum 13): exhaustive placings of the 13 clue plain letters that close the 4 loops, scored by the forced letters, best 300 completed
why: ABSCISSA has 8 letters and the K3 grid is 8 wide; length 8 is the one short repeating key that K4's clue letters do not block when both alphabets are free, and the community annealers could not detect it. Idea 99 found that at length 8 the clue cipher letters fall into two pieces (11 and 3 letters) with 4 loop checks that involve only the places of the 13 clue plain letters, and that 54 further plaintext letters are then forced.

title: Tableau with one flaw (one letter too many or too few past cell t in the header, the row labels, the strip, or one carved row such as row N) under repeating, sliding, progressive and autokey keys
why: The carved tableau has an extra L in one row, Sanborn said the K1 worksheet tableau was slightly different from the carved one and was used like a mileage chart, and his K1 key header was misspelled. If the K4 chart had one letter too many or too few in the header or in the strip, every lookup past the flaw lands one cell off. All earlier tests assume the tableau is a perfect square of shifted alphabets, so a flawed chart fails them all although the method is an ordinary one.

title: Key = two sculpture texts added or subtracted (K = T1 +- T2 + c), plus one text with a repeating or sliding word, exact hash join on the 24 clue letters
why: K2 ends LAYER TWO, Sanborn says the first three answers contain clues to the fourth and that the solver needs just to be able to read. One sculpture text as a running key is dead (best 10 of 24), and two stacked keys were closed only for repeating words and phrases. Two running texts laid over each other, for example K3 plaintext against K3 ciphertext or a K2 line against a tableau row, give a key that never repeats and that no test so far can see, yet the 24 forced key letters decide it exactly.

title: Encoder picks one of two (or three) systems per letter with a repeating or sliding key: duplicate of idea 87, which did run
why: Idea 87 failed at start-up after 7 seconds and was never tested. Scheidt masked the English language; Sanborn 1990: two separate systems; 2019: the solver needs just to be able to read. If the encoder was free at each letter to use either of two systems, whichever flattens the counts, the reader tries both and keeps the one that reads. Idea 60 tested switching between fixed rows and rule-based switching; a repeating key word with a free choice of form at every letter was never tested.

title: Fed-key models (plain/cipher autokey, idea-74 lag patterns, sculpture and K1-K3 running keys) tested on every Latin-square tableau, on one hidden alphabet, and with the key read on A-Z/KRYPTOS
why: Nearly every negative assumes the tableau is built from a keyword; the open gaps are mostly hidden alphabets. Idea 94 found a test that needs no alphabet at all: on any tableau with distinct rows and columns, the same key letter with the same plain letter must give the same cipher letter (it killed word autokey outright: T under T gives R at 28 and S at 33). Wherever the key letter inside the clues is itself a text letter, this decides the model for ALL tableaux at once, hidden ones included.

title: Close the idea-105 audit holes with fixed copies of the tests: attack 90 cipher feed 30-33 (bug), 59 cipher feed 34-60 / plain feed 7-8, 88 progressive key across word breaks (stacked keys re-checked against idea 104), 60C Slidefair same-column rule, 61 clockwise quarter turns, 69B join on key letters, 57 key letter M[s+c] / KRYPTOS[s+c]
why: Idea 105 fed textbook messages to twenty attacks and found places where K4 was never tested although the negatives say it was: a bug in attack 90, a skipped lag range in 59, progressive and stacked keys in 88, and four convention gaps. Idea 104 closed only the stacked pairs of 68, 70, 71B and 81. Each remaining hole is a region where a simple remembered-key cipher (Scheidt 2011) could still sit.

title: Key added to the message as a long number with carries (base 26 from 0 / base 27 from 1), add/sub/Beaufort, carries right-to-left and left-to-right, optional row restarts; repeating, sliding, progressive keys L 1-12
why: Scheidt: I could have moved to a different math base; the cipher is simple and can be remembered. Every exact test so far adds key and text letter by letter with no carry. If the message and the repeated key word were added as two long numbers in base 26, each cipher letter is plain + key + a carry of 0 or 1 that depends on the next letter, so the key values the clues force differ by one in an irregular way and every repeating-key test fails on a short word.

title: Known K1/K2 layer (ABSCISSA, PALIMPSEST, PALIMPCEST, KRYPTOS on the KRYPTOS or A-Z tableau, every phase, both directions, before or after) plus the full key-rule battery on a second keyword tableau
why: K2 ends LAYER TWO; Scheidt: two of the four processes are similar; the Cyrillic Projector shows Sanborn reusing the K1/K2 machine. If K4 was first run through the K2 or K1 chart (KRYPTOS tableau, ABSCISSA or PALIMPSEST) and then through a second, different chart, the clue letters seen by layer two are not EASTNORTHEAST and BERLINCLOCK, so the battery never tested the right letters. Idea 84 covered only two repeating keys; a known first layer with a sliding, progressive or autokey second layer is untested.

title: Any linear cipher-feedback rule up to 15 letters back with free coefficients (plus sparse worksheet lags to 96, plain feedback, and feedback with a repeating word of 3-5), on 666,993 keyword tableaux
why: Scheidt masked the English language with something simple that can be remembered; the simplest masks are running sums and differences (add each letter to the ones before it, or to the letter on the left and the letter above on the worksheet). Those are cipher-feedback rules with several lags at once. Earlier tests tried one lag at a time (59, 74, 90) or one cipher term (110 test B). Because all 97 cipher letters are known, every rule C[i] = P[i] + a1 C[i-1] + ... + aR C[i-R] + c can be decided in one exact solve without naming the rule.

title: Clue blocks enciphered as separate runs: free key phase at BERLINCLOCK (and at NORTHEAST) for repeating, sliding, autokey+word, progressive and two stacked keys on 666,993 keyword tableaux
why: Sanborn cut the plaintext into sentence strips and handled them out of order, and the Cyrillic Projector restarts its key at each block. If each sentence was enciphered on its own, or the sentences were enciphered in another order than they were carved, the key is continuous inside a clue but its place at the second clue is unrelated to the 42 letters between them. Idea 43 tested this only for repeating keys on 18 alphabets, idea 68 only for a gap off by 1-3; on the dictionary tableaux and for sliding, progressive and stacked keys it is untested.

title: Compass steps on a letter grid: king distance, distinct moves and compass-line moves of the 24 clue pairs on 14.5M grids
why: The first clue is itself two compass bearings, the site has a compass rose, Sanborn used matrix codes and Scheidt taught shifting matrices, and Bean found the clue plain and cipher letters unusually close in the alphabet (1 in 5,520). If the alphabet is written in a grid and the key is a string of compass moves (N, NE, E ... or stay), close letters are sideways moves and the far ones are up or down moves. Idea 97 tested small windows of shifts only in one dimension; round 6 tested grid moves only with repeating wheels.

title: Sentence key on a keyword tableau judged by growing plain and key together across the gap (beam on both strings, 20,000 best key-fragment settings)
why: Sanborn 2019: you just need to be able to read; Scheidt: the correct key word/s. A sentence used as the key on a keyword tableau was tested (ideas 57, 65, 89) only by scoring the 13 and 11 key letters the clues force, and the true key sat inside the noise in 1 of 4 planted runs, so the negative has a stated thin margin. A true setting has a property noise cannot copy: one letter further on, some plaintext letter makes BOTH the key and the message continue as English, and it keeps doing so.

title: One-letter-misspelled keyword alphabets (8.1M) and other alphabet constructions (1.7M) through the full key-rule battery, plus a Quagmire IV join for the new constructions
why: Sanborn misspells on purpose and by accident: his K1 key header reads PALIMPCEST, the text has IQLUSION, UNDERGRUUND and DESPARATLY, and K2 lost a letter. A keyword alphabet built from a misspelled word is in no dictionary, so every dictionary test would miss an otherwise ordinary cipher. Idea 86 solved arbitrary keywords only for repeating and sliding keys; the other rules (progressive, stacked, autokey, chain addition) were run on dictionary spellings only, and always with the keyword first and the rest in A-Z order.

title: Gromark (chain-addition digit keys, bases 3-16) with one dictionary keyword alphabet and the other alphabet free: exact hash join on the clue pairs
why: Bean and Scheidt's 'different math base' point to Gromark. The standard form (straight A-Z plain side) is dead by Bean. The both-hidden form survives the clues (454 base-10 primers) but was only judged by an English completion with about 50% power. Fixing one side to a dictionary keyword alphabet, as K1/K2 did, makes the test exact and the reading decisive.

title: Hidden message in the solved K1-K3 (+ Morse) text: acrostics (1st/2nd/3rd/last letter of words), every k-th word or letter (k up to 40, every start), K2 coordinate digits as step counts, carved-row first/last letters and columns, sentence initials, doubled letters; forwards and backwards; scored against word-order-shuffled texts
why: Sanborn 2005: he left instructions in the earlier text that refer to later text; 2006: the answers to the first three passages contain clues to the fourth. Wartime letter codes hid a message in the first or n-th letters of words. Earlier work used such letters only as K4 keys (ruled out); nobody here has tested whether they READ as a message, which needs no K4 and no cipher model and would give the missing method directly.

title: Two-word keys (A+B and sandwich A+B+A, repeating, every phase, L 4-26) on one hidden alphabet: true Quagmire III (C = P + K, P - K, K - P), true Quagmire II, and idea 93's numeric one-alphabet model (repeating and sliding), joined through the forced key slots and solved exactly
why: Scheidt said the key is remembered 'key word/s', and idea 93 closed single known words on a fully hidden alphabet but not two words written one after the other. On any one-alphabet tableau, S->S at 33 with K->K at 74 and R->P at 28 and 66 force equal key letters, and about 60 pairs are forced different: conditions on the key alone, which split by word.

title: Quagmire III (one arbitrary alphabet on both sides), Beaufort form, repeating key of length 18: decided exactly for every one of the 26! alphabets
why: K1 and K2 are Quagmire III on one keyed alphabet. The community's exact arbitrary-alphabet search closed the Beaufort form at every length except 13, 18, 23 and 26. Idea 86 closed 13 for every alphabet, but 18 only for keyword alphabets of up to 16 letters, because its budget ran out. 18 is the one length where an exact answer for every alphabet is still missing and is within reach.

title: Quagmire IV with two keyword alphabets of 1-9 letters (any letters, no dictionary), plain or read off by columns, repeating key 1-16, solved exactly from both alphabetical tails
why: Scheidt said the cipher runs 'with the correct key word/s', so the two alphabets of a Quagmire IV are most likely keyword alphabets. They need not be dictionary words, though: PALIMPCEST was itself a misspelling. Idea 113 left 118M placings of the 13 clue plain letters at key length 8 with no power. Idea 86 showed that a keyword alphabet is fixed by its alphabetical tail. Combining the two puts a strong prior on what was a noise search.

title: Repeating key word of 1-13 plus a steady step (per letter or once per pass, every start phase) on one hidden alphabet: both sides hidden (Vigenere, Beaufort) or one side hidden against A-Z / KRYPTOS, solved exactly mod 13 and mod 2 with distinct places required
why: Bean found the clue key values close together, and Sanborn's charts are hand tools. A key word moved on one place per pass, or a steady step added to it, is the simplest key a person remembers that is not periodic. Idea 92 tested pure formulas on a hidden alphabet and idea 86 keyword alphabets, but nobody has tested formula plus free key word with the alphabet arbitrary.

title: Two wrong clue letters (276 drop pairs: one per block at 7+ checks, both in one block at 9+): key-rule battery with idea-104 hole fixes on 666,993 keyword alphabets, multiplier+adder words (71A) and word-turned rotor (72) on 22 of the 24 clue letters
why: Sanborn says his work is 'rife with mistakes on purpose', and K1-K3 hold at least five deliberate or accidental errors (IQLUSION, UNDERGRUUND, DESPARATLY, PALIMPCEST, the dropped S). Idea 81 closed one wrong clue letter, but two mistakes in 24 letters is as likely as one at K1-K3's error rate, and two would hide the true method from every exact test run so far.

title: First part only (letters 1..E, E=49-63) under a small-number key (window 5 or 6) on a hidden plain alphabet against A-Z: free key by beam search, period 2-13 keys exactly
why: This is the one measured anomaly left. With a hidden plain alphabet against A-Z, EASTNORTHEAST alone fits a key window of 5 (0.3% of 5,000 shuffles, idea 112), BERLINCLOCK does not, and Bean's closeness is the same fact. Sanborn's 'two separate systems' allows the first part of K4 to carry a small-number key (digits, a dial) that changes regime before BERLINCLOCK.

title: Cipher-fed state device C = F(s + h(P)), s += g(C) mod 26..31: one side a dictionary keyword alphabet (other side and g hidden), and both sides any two keyword alphabets (only g hidden)
why: Idea 83 found that a cipher-fed device with every table hidden fits every modulus m >= 14, so it cannot be judged. Fixing the plain or cipher table to a keyword alphabet, as on the K1/K2 tableau, leaves about 8 exact equations. That is enough to decide a whole class of 'machine' hand ciphers that Scheidt's 'not mathematical, simple, can be remembered' allows.

title: One hidden strip used twice in the same direction, C = R[R[P+s]-s+t]-t, any wiring, solved exactly by backtracking: constant speeds, fast/slow pairs, keys of 1-5 letters (6 sampled), 21,510 theme and common words
why: Idea 82 closed two rotors where the second strip is the first read backwards, and showed that two different hidden strips cannot be judged. A hand encoder with one strip would more likely pass the letter through it twice the same way. With 26 unknown contacts against 24 clue letters this is about 5 letters over-determined, so it is decidable and was left open only because the equations are not linear.

title: Quagmire III Beaufort (one arbitrary alphabet both sides), repeating key 23 and 26: parallel-tempering English search over full alphabets with the clue equations hard; Vigenere form closed exactly
why: Idea 130 closed Quagmire III Beaufort (key = x[C]+x[P] on one hidden alphabet) for every alphabet at lengths 1-26 except 23 and 26, where K4 and many shuffles stay satisfiable; these are the last two repeating-key lengths of the K1/K2 machine with an arbitrary alphabet, so only an English score can judge them.

title: Plain autokey lags 5-12 back / 7-12 ahead on a half-hidden tableau (one dictionary alphabet, one free)
why: Idea 117 left plaintext autokey 5-12 letters back alive on every Latin-square tableau and undecided on one hidden alphabet. Ideas 90 and 100 tested only tableaux whose two sides are both known. The half-hidden form (one keyword alphabet, one written freely: Sanborn's 'modified so Scheidt couldn't decipher it') sits between the two and has enough clue equations at these lags to decide it exactly.

title: Quagmire I, II, IV (ACA definitions) with an arbitrary alphabet (pair) and a repeating key: the community's open lengths decided exactly by linear certificates mod 2/13 plus complete backtracking with distinct places
why: keithadler lists Quagmire I/II at 13, 16, 19, 20, 23, 24, 26 and Quagmire IV at 8, 13, 16, 19, 20, 23, 24, 26 as satisfiable but undecided; idea 130 showed a mod-2/mod-13 linear certificate (two letters forced to one place) decides such cases in a second, and found Quagmire III Beaufort at 18 dead that way.
